related_questions.question: What are the symptoms of vertebral artery disease?

text_blocks.snippet: Vertebral artery disease (VAD), also known as vertebrobasilar insufficiency (VBI), can cause a variety of symptoms due to reduced blood flow to the back of the brain. Common symptoms include dizziness, vertigo, visual disturbances (like double vision or blurry vision), difficulty swallowing, numbness or tingling, slurred speech, and sudden falls. In some cases, VAD can lead to a stroke or TIA.
snippet_highlighted_words: dizziness, vertigo, visual disturbances (like double vision or blurry vision), difficulty swallowing, numbness or tingling, slurred speech, and sudden falls

list.snippet: Vertigo and Dizziness: A sensation of spinning or imbalance is a frequent early symptom.
Visual Disturbances: Blurred vision, double vision, or vision loss can occur due to reduced blood flow to the areas of the brain that control vision.
Dysphagia (Difficulty Swallowing): Problems with coordinating the muscles involved in swallowing can arise.
Numbness or Tingling: This can be experienced in the face, arms, or legs.
Slurred Speech: Difficulty forming words and speaking clearly can be a symptom.
Sudden Falls (Drop Attacks): Individuals may experience unexpected falls without losing consciousness.
Headaches: Severe and persistent headaches can also occur.
Other Neurological Symptoms: Confusion, memory loss, and coordination problems can also be present.

Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) or Stroke: In severe cases, VAD can lead to a TIA (also known as a mini-stroke) or a full-blown stroke, causing more serious and potentially permanent neurological deficits.
Symptoms can vary in severity and may come and go.
Some individuals may experience only one or two of these symptoms, while others may have a combination of several.
If you experience any of these symptoms, especially if they are sudden or severe, it's crucial to seek immediate medical attention.

related_questions.question: What are the warning signs of a blocked carotid artery?

text_blocks.snippet: Warning signs of a blocked carotid artery can include transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) and stroke-like symptoms such as sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body, difficulty speaking or understanding speech, vision problems (like sudden blurred vision or loss of vision in one eye), dizziness, and severe headache. Some individuals may also experience a carotid bruit, a whooshing sound heard with a stethoscope over the artery, indicating turbulent blood flow.
snippet_highlighted_words: transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) and stroke-like symptoms such as sudden weakness or numbness on one side of the body, difficulty speaking or understanding speech, vision problems (like sudden blurred vision or loss of vision in one eye), dizziness, and severe headache

list.snippet: TIAs (Transient Ischemic Attacks): Often called "mini-strokes," TIAs are temporary disruptions of blood flow to the brain, causing stroke-like symptoms that resolve within minutes to hours.

Stroke-like symptoms: These include sudden weakness or numbness in the face, arm, or leg (often on one side of the body), difficulty speaking or understanding speech, vision problems (like blurred vision, double vision, or loss of vision in one eye), dizziness, and severe headache.
Carotid bruit: A whooshing sound heard with a stethoscope over the carotid artery, indicating turbulent blood flow due to a narrowing or blockage.
Vision problems: Sudden blurred vision, vision loss in one eye, or double vision.
Dizziness and loss of balance: Sudden dizziness or difficulty maintaining balance.
Other symptoms: Some individuals may also experience unexplained fatigue, confusion, memory loss, or difficulty thinking.

list.title: Early detection is crucial:
list.snippet: Symptoms of carotid artery disease can be subtle or even absent until a significant blockage occurs, potentially leading to a stroke.

list.title: Risk factors:
list.snippet: Factors like high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, and family history of atherosclerosis can increase the risk of carotid artery disease.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: Doctors may use a stethoscope to listen for carotid bruits, and imaging tests like ultrasound, MRI, or CT scans to assess blood flow and identify blockages.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Treatment options may include lifestyle modifications (like diet and exercise), medications (to manage risk factors and prevent blood clots), or surgical procedures (like carotid endarterectomy or carotid artery stenting) to remove or bypass blockages.

related_questions.question: What happens if the right vertebral artery is blocked?
related_questions.snippet: This is a condition called vertebral artery stenosis, also known more broadly as vertebrobasilar disease or vertebrobasilar insufficiency. Because vertebral artery stenosis can reduce or even block blood flow to your brain, it significantly increases your risk of developing a stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA).
related_questions.title: Lyerly | Neurosurgery | Vertebral Artery Stenosis - Baptist Health

text_blocks.snippet: Vertebral artery disease (VAD) occurs when the vertebral arteries, which supply blood to the back of the brain, are narrowed or blocked, potentially leading to stroke. This condition can result from atherosclerosis, where plaque buildup narrows the arteries, or from vertebral artery dissection, where a tear in the artery wall allows blood to separate the layers. Symptoms can include dizziness, visual disturbances, and difficulty with balance or speech.
snippet_highlighted_words: occurs when the vertebral arteries, which supply blood to the back of the brain, are narrowed or blocked, potentially leading to stroke

list.snippet: Atherosclerosis: This is the most common cause of VAD, where fatty deposits (plaque) build up in the arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow.
Vertebral Artery Dissection: A tear in the artery wall can disrupt blood flow and lead to stroke.
Other Risk Factors: These include age (men are more at risk before 75, women after), high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, obesity, and a family history of the condition.
Dizziness and Vertigo: A spinning sensation or loss of balance.
Visual Disturbances: Double vision, blurred vision, or vision loss.
Speech Problems: Slurred speech or difficulty forming words.
Ataxia: Difficulty with coordination and balance.
Other Symptoms: Numbness, weakness, headache, and nausea.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: Doctors may use angiography, MRI, or ultrasound to assess the vertebral arteries.
Lifestyle Changes: Quitting smoking, controlling blood pressure and cholesterol, and engaging in regular exercise.
Medications: Antiplatelet agents or anticoagulants may be prescribed to prevent blood clots.
Surgery: In some cases, procedures like angioplasty or stenting may be necessary to open up narrowed arteries.
